paragraphs: 16 submitted Parkinson disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in mitophagy (GO:0000423).

a non-intersection pathway component-induced kinase 1 (PINK1) is a mitochondrial serine/threonine kinase that monitors mitochondrial integrity and initiates mitophagy when damage is detected, and multiple studies explicitly link PINK1-dependent mitochondrial quality control to Parkinson disease pathogenesis. Beclin-1 (BECN1) is a core scaffold of the class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase complex required for autophagosome nucleation, and neuronal autophagy and mitophagy studies in Parkinson disease highlight BECN1 as part of the autophagy initiation apparatus that influences mitochondrial turnover in vulnerable neurons.

Sequestosome-1 (SQSTM1/p62) is a ubiquitin-binding cargo receptor that bridges ubiquitylated substrates to autophagosomal membranes, and it has been implicated in neuronal autophagy and mitophagy in Parkinson disease as a key determinant of whether damaged mitochondria are selectively delivered to the autophagy machinery. Unc-51 like kinase 1 (ULK1) is a serine/threonine kinase that serves as an upstream initiator of autophagy and mitophagy, and dysregulation of ULK1-dependent initiation complexes has been discussed in the context of impaired neuronal mitochondrial quality control in Parkinson disease.

The remaining proteins enriched in this term can be organized into functional clusters that support distinct steps of mitophagy. An autophagosome membrane conjugation and expansion cluster includes ATG5, MAP1LC3A, MAP1LC3B, GABARAP, GABARAPL1 and GABARAPL2, which collectively contribute to autophagosome membrane formation, a non-intersection pathway component/GABARAP lipidation and cargo enclosure around damaged mitochondria. An initiation and upstream regulatory cluster includes ULK2, TSC2 and the co-chaperone CDC37, which participate in kinase signaling and protein complex assembly that tune autophagy and mitophagy initiation in response to cellular stress. A mitochondrial dynamics and outer-membrane adaptor cluster includes DNM1L, FKBP8 and HTT, which are involved in mitochondrial fission, outer-membrane association and scaffolding functions that influence how dysfunctional mitochondria are recognized and physically prepared for sequestration by the mitophagy machinery.

Overall, enrichment of these 16 proteins in the mitophagy pathway supports a prominent role for defective mitochondrial quality control in Parkinson disease, spanning mitochondrial damage sensing, autophagy initiation, cargo selection and organelle turnover. Within this term, PINK1, BECN1 and SQSTM1 appear to be key proteins that drive the association by linking mitochondrial damage detection, autophagosome nucleation and selective cargo recruitment, respectively. A well-documented interaction relevant to this pathway is the binding of the cargo receptor SQSTM1 to a non-intersection pathway component-family proteins such as MAP1LC3A and MAP1LC3B, which helps couple ubiquitylated mitochondrial cargo to autophagosomal membranes during mitophagy. Together, these interconnected components underscore that perturbations across multiple nodes of the mitophagy network are convergently represented among Parkinson disease associated proteins in this dataset.

paragraphs: 21 submitted Parkinson disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in autophagy of mitochondrion (GO:0000422).

Among the core autophagy machinery enriched in this term, ATG12 and ATG5 form a conjugate that is essential for autophagosome membrane expansion and thus for the engulfment of damaged mitochondria during mitophagy. Their presence in this pathway alongside RB1CC1, a scaffold component of the autophagy initiation complex that organizes early steps of autophagosome formation around dysfunctional mitochondria, points to a primary disturbance at the level of autophagosome biogenesis rather than only at downstream recognition or degradation. In the context of Parkinson disease, defects affecting ATG12–ATG5 conjugation or RB1CC1-dependent initiation are consistent with impaired clearance of bioenergetically compromised mitochondria, a process emphasized in the mitophagy literature for this disorder.

ATP13A2, a lysosomal P-type ATPase, links mitochondrial autophagy to lysosomal degradative capacity, as loss-of-function mutations in ATP13A2 cause familial, early-onset parkinsonism with prominent lysosomal and mitochondrial abnormalities. Its enrichment in this pathway suggests that, in Parkinson disease, mitophagy stress may intersect with defects in cargo degradation once mitochondria have been delivered to the lysosomal compartment. PARK7 (a non-intersection pathway component) acts as an oxidative stress–responsive protein that preserves mitochondrial function and participates in the broader mitochondrial quality control network described in Parkinson disease, and its presence here is consistent with a role in buffering oxidative insults that would otherwise trigger or overwhelm mitophagy. MARK2, a microtubule affinity–regulating kinase, adds a cytoskeletal dimension to this pathway by modulating microtubule dynamics that support autophagosome trafficking and the positioning of mitochondria for efficient sequestration, thereby influencing how effectively mitophagy can proceed in vulnerable neurons.

The remaining proteins enriched in this term cluster into three functional modules. A mitophagy-initiation and nucleation cluster (BECN1, ULK1, ULK2, ATG5, ATG12, RB1CC1, TSC2) comprises regulators and scaffolds that sense nutrient and stress signals, assemble initiation complexes, and control the decision to commit damaged mitochondria to autophagic turnover. A cargo-tagging and autophagosome–mitochondrion interface cluster (PINK1, SQSTM1, MAP1LC3A, MAP1LC3B, GABARAP, GABARAPL1, GABARAPL2, HTT) includes the mitochondrial kinase PINK1, which marks dysfunctional mitochondria and is central to the Parkinson disease mitophagy literature, together with ubiquitin-binding adaptors and a non-intersection pathway component-family proteins that mediate physical coupling between tagged mitochondria and the forming autophagosomal membrane. A mitochondrial dynamics and chaperone/stress-response cluster (DNM1L, FKBP8, CDC37, MARK2) integrates fission of damaged mitochondrial segments, outer-membrane receptor functions, and chaperone-assisted signaling to coordinate structural remodeling of mitochondria with their recognition as mitophagy substrates.

Overall, enrichment of these 21 proteins in GO:0000422 supports mitochondrial autophagy as a central pathway through which genetic risk and molecular dysfunction converge in Parkinson disease. The association appears to be driven particularly by the combined presence of PINK1, ATP13A2, and PARK7, all of which are strongly linked to mitochondrial quality control and clinically to parkinsonian syndromes. Well-documented interactions between intersection proteins, such as the recruitment of SQSTM1 and a non-intersection pathway component/GABARAP family members to PINK1-labeled mitochondria, and the assembly of ULK1–RB1CC1–BECN1 initiation complexes, situate these factors within an integrated mitophagy network. These findings therefore highlight impaired recognition, sequestration, and lysosomal clearance of damaged mitochondria as a coherent mechanistic axis in Parkinson disease pathogenesis within this dataset.

paragraphs: 54 submitted Parkinson disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in autophagy (GO:0006914).

Among the enriched proteins, PINK1, LRRK2 and SQSTM1 represent well-established links between autophagy and Parkinson disease. PINK1 is a mitochondrial kinase that marks damaged mitochondria for selective autophagic removal, and pathogenic PINK1 mutations in Parkinson disease are tightly connected to impaired mitochondrial quality control within this pathway. LRRK2, a kinase frequently mutated in familial and sporadic Parkinson disease, has been shown to modulate autophagic flux and vesicle trafficking, and its kinase activity is increasingly viewed as a regulator of how neurons handle stress-induced autophagy. SQSTM1 functions as a ubiquitin-binding cargo receptor that couples polyubiquitinated substrates, including protein aggregates relevant to Parkinson pathology, to the autophagic machinery, and Parkinson-linked variants are consistent with a role in defective aggregate clearance and altered autophagy–inflammation crosstalk described in the autophagy and microglial literature.

Core autophagy scaffold and signaling proteins within the enriched set further connect general autophagy regulation to Parkinson disease. BECN1 and PIK3C3 form the canonical class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase complex that generates the phosphoinositide signals required for autophagosome nucleation, and alterations in this complex have been repeatedly implicated in Parkinson disease models that examine impaired autophagosome formation. ULK1, ULK2 and RB1CC1 constitute central components of the autophagy initiation machinery that integrates nutrient and stress cues, while TSC1, TSC2, RPTOR, RHEB, STK11 and the energy sensors PRKAA1 and PRKAA2 link this machinery to broader metabolic control; perturbation of this axis in Parkinson disease models is consistent with the notion that neurons under chronic proteotoxic and mitochondrial stress fail to mount an adequate autophagic response.

The remaining enriched proteins can be organized into functional clusters that highlight how multiple aspects of autophagy are engaged in Parkinson disease. An autophagy initiation and transcriptional control cluster includes FOXO1, FOXO3, STK11, PRKAA1, PRKAA2, RPTOR, RHEB, TSC1, TSC2, MARK2, TBK1 and TRAF6, which together reflect nutrient sensing, stress-activated kinase signaling and transcriptional programs known to tune autophagy levels in response to cellular stress. An autophagosome membrane dynamics and cargo-handling cluster includes ATG5, ATG12, GABARAP, GABARAPL1, GABARAPL2, MAP1LC3A, MAP1LC3B, TECPR1, UVRAG, WDFY3, WDR6, CHMP4B, VPS26A, UBQLN1, UBQLN4 and UCHL1, representing conjugation systems, a non-intersection pathway component/GABARAP family proteins, accessory factors for autophagosome maturation, endosomal sorting components and ubiquitin-binding shuttles that together support selective recognition and delivery of damaged proteins and organelles to autophagosomes. A mitochondrial and membrane quality-control cluster encompasses ATP13A2, ATP2A2, DNM1L, LRPPRC, ANXA7, DDRGK1, FKBP8, PARK7 and HTT, aligning lysosomal cation transport, calcium handling, mitochondrial fission and chaperone-like protection with autophagic removal of dysfunctional mitochondria and membranes. Finally, a proteostasis, chaperone and inflammatory-modulation cluster includes HSP90AA1, HSPB1, CDC37, GAPDH, IKBKG, RALB, STK38L and IFT88, integrating molecular chaperones, kinase co-chaperones and inflammatory signaling adaptors that influence both the folding environment and the balance between autophagy, apoptosis and neuroinflammatory responses described in Parkinson disease autophagy studies.

Together, enrichment of these 54 proteins in the autophagy pathway indicates that multiple tiers of the autophagic system—initiation, cargo selection, vesicle dynamics, mitochondrial quality control and stress–inflammation integration—are collectively engaged in Parkinson disease. Within this network, PINK1, LRRK2 and SQSTM1 appear to drive the association by linking genetic risk and aggregate/mitochondrial handling directly to autophagic processes in neurons and glia. Well-documented interactions among the enriched proteins, such as formation of the BECN1–PIK3C3 complex that nucleates autophagosomes and the cooperation of ULK1 with RB1CC1 at the initiation step, reinforce the idea that coordinated dysfunction across autophagy modules, rather than isolated lesions, underlies impaired proteostasis and neurodegeneration in Parkinson disease. These findings support the view that modulating autophagy at multiple regulatory nodes may be necessary to restore effective clearance of damaged cellular components in the Parkinsonian brain.

pathways.pathway_description: The autophagic process that proceeds via the formation of an autophagosome. [PMID:24366339]
pathways.cell_context: Nigral dopaminergic neurons, given the convergence of macroautophagy genes (ATG5/ATG12, BECN1, GABARAP family), PD gene ATP13A2, and HTT on autophagic clearance of toxic protein aggregates and dysfunctional mitochondria.
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: Macroautophagy is a major degradative pathway that sequesters cytoplasmic material into autophagosomes, and its impairment is a central mechanism in PD by limiting clearance of damaged mitochondria and aggregated proteins such as alpha-synuclein. Both insufficient and dysregulated macroautophagy can promote toxic accumulation of substrates and neuronal death in PD.
Intersection-gene interpretation: ATG5, ATG12, and BECN1 are core components of the autophagosome formation machinery, while ATP13A2 and ATP2A2 are ATP-dependent transporters that influence lysosomal and ER calcium homeostasis, respectively, thereby affecting autophagosome maturation and fusion. These intersection genes define key steps from autophagosome biogenesis to lysosomal function that, when perturbed, can drive PD-related proteostatic and organellar stress.
PubMed literature synthesis: The review on the LRRK2–macroautophagy axis directly links macroautophagy to a major genetic form of PD, highlighting how LRRK2 modulates autophagosome dynamics. The study on small molecule-driven NLRP3 inhibition via interplay between ubiquitination and autophagy and the LAMP2 isoform review further support that macroautophagy intersects with inflammatory signaling and lysosomal receptor systems relevant to PD pathology.
Cell/tissue context: The macroautophagy literature and LRRK2-focused work primarily implicate neurons and glial cells within the CNS, especially dopaminergic neurons that are vulnerable in Parkinson disease. [PMID:30966861] [PMID:37469132] [PMID:28202669]

paragraphs: 39 submitted Parkinson disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in ubiquitin protein ligase binding (GO:0031625).

Within this enriched set, PINK1, SQSTM1 and BECN1 exemplify how ubiquitin ligase binding intersects with mitochondrial and autophagic dysfunction in Parkinson disease. PINK1 is a mitochondrial kinase that recruits and organizes ubiquitin ligase activity on damaged mitochondria by binding E3 enzymes at the outer mitochondrial membrane, linking this pathway directly to mitophagy deficits in Parkinson pathology. SQSTM1 is a ubiquitin-binding scaffold that also interacts with multiple E3 ligases, positioning ubiquitinated cargo for degradation and thereby connecting ubiquitin ligase signaling to selective autophagy of misfolded proteins and damaged organelles in dopaminergic neurons. BECN1, previously noted for its role in autophagy, contributes here through its capacity to assemble ubiquitin ligase–containing complexes that modulate autophagosome formation, further embedding ubiquitin ligase binding within autophagic control in Parkinson disease.

The deubiquitinase UCHL1 and the ubiquitin-editing enzyme OTUB1 link ubiquitin protein ligase binding to the dynamic remodeling of ubiquitin chains in Parkinson disease. UCHL1, which is genetically and pathologically implicated in Parkinson disease, binds to ubiquitin ligase systems and regulates the availability and turnover of ubiquitin conjugates at synapses and in neuronal soma, so that perturbations in its ligase-binding interactions can favor accumulation of aggregation-prone proteins. OTUB1 binds specific E3 ligases and modulates their activity by cleaving or blocking ubiquitin chains, creating a sensitive rheostat on ligase output that may influence how neurons respond to proteotoxic and inflammatory stress in Parkinson disease. TRIM28, a a non-intersection pathway component-type ubiquitin ligase and transcriptional corepressor that itself engages in E3–E3 and E3–substrate binding, provides an additional nuclear node where altered ubiquitin ligase binding can reshape chromatin-associated ubiquitination and transcriptional programs relevant to neuronal survival.

RIPK1, TRAF2 and IKBKG illustrate how ubiquitin ligase binding feeds into inflammatory and cell-death signaling relevant to Parkinson disease. RIPK1 is a kinase whose function is tightly controlled by its interaction with ubiquitin ligases that decorate it with specific ubiquitin chains; its binding to these ligases determines whether cells engage pro-survival, apoptotic or necroptotic programs that can shape neurodegeneration. TRAF2 is an adaptor with intrinsic ubiquitin ligase activity that binds other E3 ligases as well as receptor-associated complexes, promoting polyubiquitin scaffolds that propagate stress and inflammatory signaling, processes increasingly recognized in Parkinson pathology. IKBKG, the regulatory subunit of the NF-κB kinase complex, binds multiple ubiquitin ligases and their chains, acting as a hub that translates ubiquitin ligase–dependent signaling into transcriptional responses that can either protect or injure vulnerable nigral neurons depending on context.

AURKA, DNM1L and FOXO1 connect ubiquitin ligase binding to cell-cycle–independent neuronal functions, mitochondrial dynamics and transcriptional stress responses in Parkinson disease. AURKA, although classically a mitotic kinase, binds specific ubiquitin ligases that regulate its stability and non-mitotic signaling functions in mature neurons, where altered turnover could influence cytoskeletal organization and survival pathways. DNM1L, already implicated in mitochondrial fission, engages ubiquitin ligases that modify its activity and turnover at mitochondria, thereby tying imbalanced fission–fusion dynamics in Parkinson disease to E3-dependent control. FOXO1 is a transcription factor whose stability and activity depend on its interaction with ubiquitin ligases, and its ligase-binding–driven regulation of genes involved in oxidative stress resistance and autophagy is likely to modulate neuronal resilience in the Parkinsonian brain.

The remaining enriched proteins can be grouped into functional clusters that highlight how ubiquitin ligase binding is embedded across proteostasis, signaling and organelle quality control. A chaperone–co-chaperone cluster comprising HSP90AA1, HSP90AB1, HSPA1A, HSPA1B, HSPA1L, HSPA5, HSPBP1, DNAJA1, TCP1, BAG2 and BAG6 underscores that many molecular chaperones and their regulators bind ubiquitin ligases to couple client recognition with ubiquitination and degradation of misfolded proteins. An autophagy–cargo receptor cluster formed by GABARAP, GABARAPL1, GABARAPL2, MAP1LC3A, MAP1LC3B, SNCAIP, CAMLG and ERLIN2 points to ligase-binding adaptors that bridge ubiquitinated cargo, including synaptic and membrane proteins, to autophagosomal membranes. A signaling adaptor cluster including IKBKE, TANK, TRAF2 and RIPK1 emphasizes ubiquitin ligase–dependent assembly of innate immune and NF-κB signaling complexes. Finally, a group of regulatory and scaffolding proteins composed of CACYBP, LRPPRC, PRKACA, RALB, BAG6, YWHAE and YWHAZ illustrates how 14-3-3 proteins, GTPases, kinases and multipurpose scaffolds bind E3 ligases to fine-tune phosphorylation–ubiquitination crosstalk, mitochondrial RNA handling and vesicular trafficking processes implicated in Parkinson disease.

Together, the enrichment of exactly 39 proteins in ubiquitin protein ligase binding indicates that Parkinson disease–related genes converge on a shared capacity to bind ubiquitin E3 ligases, constraining the affected activity class to ubiquitin-focused binding rather than a single downstream pathway. The pattern of intersection suggests that aberrant engagement of ubiquitin ligases at mitochondria, autophagic membranes and inflammatory signaling complexes is a recurrent theme, with PINK1, SQSTM1 and UCHL1 emerging as key drivers of this association. Well-documented interactions among the listed proteins, such as SQSTM1 binding to MAP1LC3A, MAP1LC3B and GABARAP family members, or a non-intersection pathway component chaperones stabilizing client kinases like AURKA and RIPK1 in ligase-regulated complexes, support a model in which coordinated but vulnerable ubiquitin ligase binding networks shape neuronal fate in Parkinson disease. These findings therefore highlight ubiquitin ligase engagement itself as a potential point of therapeutic intervention across multiple pathogenic mechanisms in the disorder.

paragraphs: 28 submitted Parkinson disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in a non-intersection pathway component-activated protein kinase activity (GO:0004679).

Within this molecular function term, the core a non-intersection pathway component-activated protein kinase catalytic subunits PRKAA1 and PRKAA2 are the principal effectors, catalyzing a non-intersection pathway component-dependent phosphorylation of downstream targets. Both subunits have been implicated in neuronal energy sensing and stress responses in Parkinson disease models, where altered a non-intersection pathway component signaling has been linked to autophagy modulation and vulnerability of dopaminergic neurons under metabolic and oxidative stress conditions.

The upstream kinase STK11 provides a direct regulatory input into this activity, functioning as a major activating kinase for PRKAA1/2 and thereby coupling cellular energy status to a non-intersection pathway component-driven phosphorylation. In Parkinson disease-relevant systems, dysregulation of STK11-dependent activation of a non-intersection pathway component has been reported to influence neuronal survival pathways and autophagic flux, positioning STK11 as an important modulator of a non-intersection pathway component-activated protein kinase signaling in the affected brain regions.

Several additional kinases enriched in this term interface with a non-intersection pathway component-activated protein kinase activity through autophagy and stress-response signaling. ULK1 and ULK2, previously noted in this report, are well-characterized substrates and partners of a non-intersection pathway component that initiate autophagosome formation, and their inclusion here supports a link between a non-intersection pathway component-dependent phosphorylation and autophagy initiation in Parkinson disease. TBK1 participates in stress-induced autophagy and mitophagy signaling and has been connected to neurodegenerative mechanisms in which a non-intersection pathway component–ULK1 pathways are engaged. PINK1, also previously discussed, converges on mitochondrial quality control and can intersect functionally with a non-intersection pathway component–driven mitophagy cascades in neuronal cells under mitochondrial stress.

A second group of enriched kinases centers on cell stress, inflammation, and necroptotic cell death, processes that can be modulated by a non-intersection pathway component-activated kinase signaling. RIPK1, RIPK3 and RIPK4 are key mediators of programmed necrosis and inflammatory signaling; their presence alongside PRKAA1/2 suggests that a non-intersection pathway component-dependent kinase activity is positioned to influence, or be influenced by, necroptotic pathways in Parkinson disease models. IRAK1 connects innate immune receptor signaling to downstream kinase cascades and has been linked to inflammatory responses relevant to neurodegeneration. LRRK2, a major Parkinson disease kinase, integrates vesicular trafficking and inflammatory signaling and has been reported to functionally crosstalk with cellular energy and autophagy pathways in which a non-intersection pathway component is central.

The remaining proteins enriched in this pathway can be organized into functional clusters that flank the core a non-intersection pathway component-activated kinase holoenzyme. One cluster comprises a non-intersection pathway component regulatory subunits PRKAB2, PRKAG2 and PRKAG3, which contribute β and γ components required for a non-intersection pathway component sensing and proper kinase activation. A second cluster includes autophagy- and apoptosis-related Ste20 family kinases STK3, STK4, STK24 and STK38L, which participate in stress and death signaling pathways that can intersect with a non-intersection pathway component-mediated decisions on cell survival and autophagy. A third group contains kinases linked to cytoskeletal dynamics and cell polarity, such as MARK2 (previously noted), MAST3, NEK1 and LATS1, suggesting that a non-intersection pathway component-activated phosphorylation interfaces with microtubule organization and centrosomal function in vulnerable neuronal populations. Additional stress-responsive kinases, including RPS6KA1, SGK1, KSR1, AURKA, TNIK and a non-intersection pathway component-family–related signaling via TBK1, further broaden the spectrum of a non-intersection pathway component-sensitive phosphorylation cascades captured within this term.

Overall, enrichment of these 28 proteins in a non-intersection pathway component-activated protein kinase activity indicates that a non-intersection pathway component-dependent phosphorylation is a central biochemical activity modulating energy sensing, autophagy, inflammatory signaling and stress-induced cell death in Parkinson disease. The association appears to be driven primarily by the canonical a non-intersection pathway component catalytic subunits PRKAA1 and PRKAA2 together with their upstream activator STK11, which collectively anchor the term’s mechanistic relevance. Well-documented signaling interactions, particularly phosphorylation of ULK1 by PRKAA1/2 downstream of STK11, provide a coherent link between a non-intersection pathway component-activated kinase activity and autophagy initiation. These coordinated kinase activities suggest that perturbation of a non-intersection pathway component-sensitive phosphorylation nodes may be a common mechanism contributing to neuronal vulnerability and degeneration in Parkinson disease.

paragraphs: 22 submitted Parkinson disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in autophagosome (GO:0005776).

Among the proteins enriched in this term, BECN1, ULK1 and RB1CC1 exemplify core components of the autophagosome initiation machinery that physically localize to the forming autophagosomal membrane. ULK1 is a serine/threonine kinase that operates at the earliest steps of autophagosome biogenesis, and its recruitment to the autophagosome is a key event in controlling vesicle nucleation in neurons affected by Parkinson disease. BECN1 participates in the autophagosome-localized class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase complex, and altered BECN1-dependent autophagosome formation has been repeatedly implicated in autophagy–lysosome dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease models. RB1CC1, which co-localizes with ULK1 at the autophagosome, serves as a scaffold for the initiation complex, and changes in this complex are consistent with the broader pattern of impaired macroautophagy observed in Parkinson disease brains and experimental systems.

LRRK2, ATP13A2 and HTT highlight how proteins with distinct primary functions can converge at the autophagosome in Parkinson disease–relevant contexts. LRRK2, a kinase mutated in familial Parkinson disease, has been observed within autophagosome-related structures, consistent with experimental data linking LRRK2 activity to altered autophagosome dynamics. ATP13A2, a lysosomal P-type ATPase whose deficiency is linked to early-onset parkinsonism, localizes to the autophagosome–lysosome interface, and its dysfunction aligns with reports that environmental stressors in dopaminergic neurons disrupt autophagosome–lysosome fusion. HTT, although best known for its role in another neurodegenerative disorder, is also recruited to autophagosomes where it modulates cargo handling, and perturbation of this function has been connected to the broader theme of autophagy–lysosome pathway failure in Parkinson disease models.

SQSTM1, WDFY3 and TECPR1 illustrate how cargo-selective adaptors and scaffolds accumulate on the autophagosome surface in Parkinson disease–relevant settings. SQSTM1 is a ubiquitin-binding autophagy receptor that co-localizes with autophagosomal membrane proteins and selectively delivers ubiquitylated proteins and organelles for degradation; the aggregation of SQSTM1-positive autophagosomes is a frequent marker of impaired macroautophagy in neurodegenerative disease tissue. WDFY3, a large scaffold protein associated with selective degradation of neuronal cargo, localizes to autophagosomes in neurons and is consistent with the accumulation of defective or misfolded proteins in Parkinson disease. TECPR1 is similarly enriched at autophagosomes and has been linked to the efficiency of autophagosome maturation, fitting with experimental observations that pharmacological agents promoting autophagosome formation can ameliorate pathology in Parkinson disease models driven by misfolded proteins.

The remaining proteins enriched in the autophagosome term fall into several functional clusters that each occupy characteristic positions within this compartment. One cluster comprises the ATG12–ATG5 conjugation system and the a non-intersection pathway component/GABARAP family (ATG12, ATG5, MAP1LC3A, MAP1LC3B, GABARAP, GABARAPL1, GABARAPL2), which are covalently or tightly associated with autophagosomal membranes and act as structural and adaptor components of the autophagosome rather than stable cytosolic residents. A second cluster includes the ubiquitin-like cargo shuttling proteins UBQLN1 and UBQLN4, which can be transiently recruited to autophagosomes as they escort misfolded or aggregation-prone proteins toward degradation. A third cluster encompasses CHMP4B and UVRAG, proteins that participate in membrane remodeling and autophagosome maturation or fusion and that are therefore positioned at the interface between autophagosomes and lysosomes. PIK3C3, although primarily a lipid kinase, is enriched on autophagosomal membranes where it generates phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate to support vesicle nucleation, while ULK2 provides additional kinase activity at the forming autophagosome. ATP13A2, beyond its role noted above, functionally aligns with these maturation and fusion factors, underscoring that many of the proteins in this term are transient residents that cycle on and off the autophagosome as it matures, in contrast to more stably autophagosome-embedded proteins such as the a non-intersection pathway component/GABARAP family. As with all GO cellular component annotations, these proteins are enriched in the autophagosome as a shared subcellular location, and this co-localization alone is not evidence that they act through a single, unified disease mechanism.

Overall, enrichment of Parkinson disease–linked proteins in the autophagosome compartment points to this double-membrane vesicle as a key anatomical site at which neurodegenerative pathology manifests, through defects in autophagosome formation, cargo recruitment and fusion with lysosomes. The pattern is driven in particular by core initiation and scaffold proteins such as BECN1, ULK1 and SQSTM1, whose autophagosomal localization anchors much of the observed dysfunction. Well-documented interactions among the proteins listed for this record, including the formation of ULK1–RB1CC1 complexes at the nascent autophagosome, assembly of PIK3C3-containing complexes with BECN1 at the isolation membrane, and binding of SQSTM1 to MAP1LC3A/MAP1LC3B and GABARAP family proteins on the autophagosomal surface, support a model in which multiple steps of the autophagosome life cycle are vulnerable in Parkinson disease. Although the GO:0005776 result itself reflects shared localization rather than directionality or regulation, the convergence of these interactions within the autophagosome compartment is consistent with broader evidence that macroautophagy failure is a central component of Parkinson disease pathology.

paragraphs:
Exactly 52 Parkinson disease associated proteins were significantly enriched in the mitochondrion (GO:0005739) cellular component term.

Within this term, PINK1, PARK7 and LRRK2 stand out as mitochondrial proteins with well-established links to Parkinson disease. PINK1 is a mitochondrial kinase that accumulates on damaged mitochondria and participates in mitochondrial quality control pathways discussed extensively in the Parkinson disease literature, directly connecting this compartment to disease-relevant surveillance of organelle integrity. PARK7 is a redox-sensitive protein enriched at mitochondria that contributes to buffering oxidative stress and preserving mitochondrial function in models of neurodegeneration. LRRK2 has been reported to influence mitochondrial homeostasis and respiration, and its enrichment in the mitochondrion term underscores that a substantial fraction of the Parkinson disease protein module converges on this organelle as a site of pathogenic vulnerability.

Several other enriched proteins participate in mitochondrion-centered degradation pathways that have been implicated in Parkinson disease–related mitochondrial quality control. BECN1, SQSTM1 and MAP1LC3B are core components of the autophagy machinery that can be recruited to mitochondria during selective elimination of dysfunctional organelles, and mitochondrial quality control has been highlighted as a key theme in Parkinson disease. Their co-enrichment with PINK1 in the mitochondrial compartment supports the view that both damage sensing and downstream degradative responses are physically organized around this organelle in disease-relevant contexts. GABARAPL1 and ULK1, which also localize to mitochondria, further connect membrane dynamics around damaged mitochondria to upstream autophagy initiation.

Proteins involved in mitochondrial dynamics and stress signaling further emphasize this organelle as a nexus of Parkinson disease pathology. DNM1L is a central mediator of mitochondrial fission whose presence in the enriched set is consistent with reports that altered fission–fusion balance accompanies mitochondrial dysfunction in Parkinson disease models. SOD1, although classically associated with superoxide detoxification, is annotated to the mitochondrion and links oxidative stress at this site to broader neurodegenerative processes discussed in comparative reviews of Parkinson disease and related disorders. MAVS, a signaling adaptor on the outer mitochondrial membrane, provides a direct physical bridge between mitochondrial distress and innate immune pathways that have been described as part of a broader “cell danger response” in neurodegeneration.

The remaining proteins enriched in the mitochondrion term can be organized into functional clusters that reflect distinct aspects of mitochondrial biology. A first cluster comprises additional mediators of mitochondrial dynamics and organelle quality control, including DNM1L, FKBP8, BECN1, SQSTM1, MAP1LC3B, GABARAPL1 and ULK1, which together connect membrane remodeling, cargo recognition and autophagosome formation at the organelle surface. A second cluster contains mitochondrial chaperones and proteostasis factors such as HSP90AA1, HSP90AB1, HSPA1A, HSPA1B, HSPA4, HSPA5, HYOU1, DNAJA1 and CANX, which support protein folding and stress responses in close proximity to the organelle. A third cluster is composed of metabolic and redox-regulating proteins, including DLD, HSD17B10, PKM, SOD1, C1QBP, BCKDK, GARS1, KARS1, LRPPRC and CCDC90B, reflecting mitochondrial roles in energy metabolism and oxidative balance that are frequently disrupted in Parkinson disease. A fourth cluster is made up of signaling and scaffolding proteins enriched at the mitochondrion, such as STK11, MARK2, PRKACA, RIPK1, SGK1, CDK1, PPP1R15A, PPP2R1A, PPP2R2B, YAP1, YWHAE, YWHAG, YWHAH, NFKB1 and IKBKE, which can transduce mitochondrial status to broader cellular signaling networks. Additional proteins including DDX3X, DISC1, LRRC59, LCA5, C1QBP and MAVS form a cluster of outer-membrane adaptors and RNA- or membrane-associated factors that position the mitochondrion within trafficking and stress-sensing pathways. In all cases, the GO:CC annotation indicates that these proteins are enriched in the mitochondrial compartment, but many of them are transient residents rather than structural constituents of the organelle, and co-localization alone does not imply that they share a single pathogenic mechanism.

Overall, enrichment of exactly 52 Parkinson disease associated proteins in the mitochondrion term highlights this organelle as a major subcellular site where genetic and molecular risk converges, consistent with extensive evidence that mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired quality control are central features of Parkinson disease pathology. The association appears to be driven in particular by PINK1, PARK7 and LRRK2, whose roles in mitochondrial fidelity, oxidative stress handling and organelle homeostasis have been directly linked to Parkinson disease. Well-documented interactions between PINK1 and autophagy-related proteins such as SQSTM1 and MAP1LC3B, together with the presence of DNM1L and multiple mitochondrial chaperones, suggest that damage sensing, organelle remodeling and proteostatic stress responses all occur within this shared compartment. Because GO:CC terms describe localization rather than mechanism, these results indicate that many Parkinson disease related proteins act in or at the mitochondrion, but additional functional data are required to dissect which specific pathways within this organelle drive neurodegeneration.

paragraphs: 3 submitted Parkinson disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Lewy body (GO:0097413).

PINK1 is a mitochondrial Ser/Thr kinase that becomes stabilized on depolarized mitochondria and initiates mitophagy signaling. In the context of Parkinson disease, loss-of-function variants in PINK1 are firmly linked to familial early-onset parkinsonism, and experimental models consistently show that impaired PINK1 activity compromises mitochondrial quality control in dopaminergic neurons. Immunohistochemical studies have reported PINK1 signal in or around Lewy body–bearing neurons, supporting the annotation of PINK1 to this term as a transient resident that is recruited to damaged mitochondria within the cytoplasmic milieu where Lewy bodies form rather than as a structural component of the inclusion itself.

SQSTM1 encodes the ubiquitin-binding scaffold protein p62, which functions as an autophagy receptor by binding both polyubiquitinated cargo and a non-intersection pathway component-family proteins on the autophagosome membrane. In Parkinson disease and related Lewy body disorders, p62 is a well-recognized component of ubiquitin-positive neuronal inclusions, and robust p62 immunoreactivity is routinely used as a histopathological marker of Lewy bodies alongside ubiquitin and alpha-synuclein. Within this pathway, SQSTM1 is therefore best interpreted as a structural constituent of the Lewy body inclusion that accumulates as part of an attempted, but incomplete, autophagic response to misfolded and aggregated proteins.

ATF4 is a stress-responsive transcription factor that is induced by the integrated stress response downstream of eIF2α phosphorylation and regulates genes involved in redox balance, amino acid metabolism, and cell fate under chronic stress. In experimental Parkinson disease models, ATF4 upregulation has been associated with endoplasmic reticulum and oxidative stress in dopaminergic neurons, and ATF4 immunoreactivity has been observed in neurons in affected regions, including those harboring proteinaceous inclusions. Within the Lewy body pathway, ATF4 is most plausibly a transient resident of the diseased neuronal cytoplasm and nucleus that reflects activation of stress signaling in Lewy body–bearing neurons rather than a core structural constituent of the inclusions themselves.

When interpreted as a Cellular Component term, enrichment of these proteins in the Lewy body pathway indicates that they co-localize to the cytoplasmic inclusion compartment or its immediate microenvironment, not that they share a single molecular mechanism. Lewy bodies represent a specialized pathological site where structural inclusion components such as SQSTM1 accumulate together with stress signaling factors like ATF4 and quality-control kinases such as PINK1. Notably, functional coupling between PINK1-dependent mitochondrial quality control and SQSTM1-mediated autophagic cargo recognition has been documented, providing a mechanistic link between mitochondrial damage and the ubiquitin–p62–positive inclusions that typify Parkinson disease and related Lewy body dementias. Overall, this pathway highlights Lewy bodies as a convergence point where PINK1 and SQSTM1 appear to drive the association through their established roles in mitochondrial and proteostatic quality control, with ATF4 marking the accompanying integrated stress response; however, their co-localization within Lewy body–bearing neurons should be interpreted as evidence of shared pathological context rather than, on its own, proof of a unified pathogenic mechanism.

paragraphs: 80 submitted Parkinson disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in microtubule cytoskeleton (GO:0015630).

Among the enriched proteins with well-established links to Parkinson pathology, LRRK2 is notable as a kinase that binds to and regulates microtubule-associated complexes, influencing organelle trafficking along axons. Pathogenic LRRK2 variants have been widely implicated in familial and sporadic Parkinson disease, and accumulating experimental evidence indicates that LRRK2 can alter microtubule organization and the dynamics of microtubule-based transport in neurons, providing a direct connection between this enriched compartment and neuronal vulnerability. DNM1L, a central mediator of mitochondrial fission that also associates with microtubule-dependent mitochondrial trafficking, further connects the microtubule cytoskeleton to the impaired mitochondrial dynamics described in Parkinson models, where defects in organelle movement along axonal microtubules contribute to synaptic failure. HTT, although classically linked to another neurodegenerative disorder, is a microtubule-interacting scaffold that modulates vesicle and organelle transport; its presence in this enriched set underscores that microtubule-dependent trafficking pathways affected in Parkinson disease intersect with broader neurodegeneration-related transport machinery.

Several additional microtubule-associated regulators in the enriched set are implicated in neuronal structure and stress responses relevant to Parkinson disease. CRMP1 is an axonal guidance and neurite outgrowth factor that binds tubulin heterodimers and influences microtubule assembly; alterations in CRMP1 function can destabilize axons and may sensitize dopaminergic projections to the microtubule-destabilizing events described in toxin-based Parkinson models. MICAL1, an oxidoreductase that directly modifies cytoskeletal elements to promote microtubule and actin disassembly, provides a biochemical route through which oxidative stress—a hallmark of Parkinson pathology—could be translated into structural disruption of the microtubule cytoskeleton. NEK1, a kinase localized to centrosomes and microtubules, participates in microtubule organization and ciliary function, and its enrichment here suggests that centrosome- and cilium-associated components of the microtubule network contribute to the cellular environments in which Parkinson-relevant stress signaling and protein handling occur.

Mitotic and centrosomal regulators enriched in this term point to the centrosome and spindle apparatus as key microtubule-based compartments intersecting Parkinson disease biology. AURKA, PLK1, CDC25B, CDK1, CEP170, CEP19, CEP44, CETN2, CNTROB, KIF14, NEK1, and LATS1 are all core components or regulators of centrosomes, spindle poles, or kinetochore-attached microtubules. Although many of these proteins are classically studied in dividing cells, they persist in post-mitotic neurons as structural or regulatory constituents of the microtubule-organizing center and primary cilium, compartments that can modulate neuronal polarity and signal transduction. Their enrichment in the microtubule cytoskeleton term in a Parkinson-associated module indicates that centrosomal and spindle-derived microtubule arrays, rather than microtubules in general, form one of the principal subcellular sites in which these risk- and pathology-linked proteins co-localize.

A second functional cluster consists of autophagy- and endolysosomal pathway components that engage microtubules for cargo trafficking. GABARAP, GABARAPL1, MAP1LC3A, MAP1LC3B, and CHMP4B, previously discussed in the context of membrane remodeling and degradative pathways, appear here specifically as microtubule-associated adaptors that decorate autophagosomes and endosomal membranes moving along axonal microtubules. APPBP2, ERC1, LRPPRC, and MME similarly participate in cargo sorting, vesicle tethering, or organelle homeostasis in ways that depend on efficient microtubule-based transport. These proteins are not structural tubulin components but transient or peripheral residents of the microtubule cytoskeleton, recruited to microtubule tracks or microtubule-anchored membranes to couple degradation, signaling, and metabolism to long-range intracellular transport in neurons affected in Parkinson disease.

A third cluster is formed by chaperones and protein quality control factors that concentrate along microtubules and at microtubule-associated complexes. The a non-intersection pathway component chaperonin subunits (CCT3, CCT4, CCT5, CCT6A, CCT7), HSPA1A, HSPA1B, HSPA2, HSPB1, DNAJA1, BAG2, HSF1, NUDCD3, and GAPDH assemble near microtubules to fold cytoskeletal and trafficking proteins, to refold or triage damaged proteins that accumulate along axons, and to stabilize microtubule-dependent complexes under stress. Their enrichment reflects the fact that the microtubule cytoskeleton functions not only as a structural scaffold but also as a platform where chaperone-mediated surveillance of misfolded proteins occurs in Parkinson-relevant neurons. Additional proteins such as AJUBA, CBY1, PATJ, PLEKHA7, ILK, EPB41L3, EMD, IKBKG, CYLD, ATF4, DYRK1A, DISC1, DDX3X, CIAO1, IFT88, LCA5, MLF1, and LATS1 localize to cortical microtubule arrays, cell–cell junctions, cilia, and signaling hubs, where they integrate cytoskeletal organization with inflammatory, stress-responsive, and polarity pathways implicated in Parkinson disease. Within this enriched term, some of these proteins are stable structural residents of microtubule-containing complexes (for example, centrosomal and ciliary scaffolds), whereas many others are transient residents that are recruited dynamically to microtubule-associated sites.

Overall, the enrichment of Parkinson disease associated proteins in the microtubule cytoskeleton term indicates that a substantial fraction of the implicated proteome co-localizes to microtubule-based structures where axonal transport, organelle positioning, and protein quality control converge, a compartment that has been repeatedly highlighted as a site of pathology by studies of microtubule destabilization and toxin-induced Tau phosphorylation in Parkinson models. Within this result, LRRK2, DNM1L, and HTT appear to be key drivers because they directly couple microtubule-dependent trafficking to neuronal survival pathways that are disrupted in Parkinson disease. The presence of multiple centrosomal kinases (such as AURKA and PLK1) and axonal regulators (such as CRMP1 and MICAL1) alongside autophagy adaptors (for example, GABARAP, GABARAPL1, and MAP1LC3B) illustrates that structural microtubule elements and degradative pathways are physically and functionally intertwined in this compartment. Importantly, this enrichment reflects a shared localization to the microtubule cytoskeleton and its associated complexes; co-localization alone is not evidence of a single shared mechanism, but it does highlight the microtubule network as a critical anatomical substrate on which diverse Parkinson-related processes intersect and potentially interact.

LRRK2 functions as a kinase embedded in the signal transduction segment of the pathway, where it modulates downstream cytoskeletal and vesicular processes and is a well-established genetic determinant of familial and sporadic Parkinson disease. PINK1 is positioned on the mitochondrial branch of the map as a kinase that senses mitochondrial damage and initiates downstream quality-control responses, forming part of a directed route from stress inputs to mitochondrial dysfunction. PARK7 is mapped alongside PINK1 at the mitochondrial and oxidative stress node, where its redox-sensitive chaperone-like activity integrates oxidative insults with the maintenance of mitochondrial integrity in dopaminergic neurons.

Proteostasis-related components in this intersection are distributed along the protein quality-control arm of the KEGG pathway, interfacing with mitochondrial and synaptic branches. UCHL1 is a deubiquitinating enzyme enriched in the ubiquitin-dependent protein degradation segment, where it regulates ubiquitin recycling and is repeatedly implicated in Parkinson disease through its impact on neuronal protein turnover. SNCAIP is placed on the synaptic and aggregation-related portion of the map, where it binds aggregation-prone proteins and contributes to the handling of misfolded species in affected neurons. HSPA5, an endoplasmic reticulum chaperone, lies upstream in the unfolded protein response and protein folding module, forming part of a directed route that connects ER stress to downstream neuronal dysfunction and cross-talks with the KEGG protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum pathway.

The remaining enriched proteins cluster into functional groups along the downstream effector zones of the KEGG Parkinson disease map. An oxidative stress and thiol-redox cluster, comprising SOD1 and TXN, is localized to the mitochondrial and cytosolic antioxidant defense branch, where it connects directly to nodes that cross-talk with KEGG oxidative phosphorylation and other reactive oxygen species–handling pathways. A cytoskeletal and axonal transport cluster, including TUBA1C, TUBB1, TUBB2A, TUBB2B and TUBB3, aligns with the microtubule-dependent transport arm downstream of signaling kinases, supporting the integrity of axons and synaptic terminals mapped in KEGG, and providing potential cross-talk to axon-guidance and synaptic-function pathways. A stress-responsive transcriptional cluster is represented by ATF4, which appears in the ER stress and integrated stress response segment downstream of HSPA5, where it relays chronic stress into altered gene expression programs relevant to neuronal vulnerability. Finally, PRKACA forms a signaling kinase cluster residing in the cAMP-dependent signaling portion of the map, linking upstream neurotransmitter and receptor inputs to phosphorylation of downstream effectors and intersecting with adjacent KEGG cAMP signaling modules.

Taken together, enrichment of these 15 proteins in KEGG:05012 indicates that the submitted module converges on mitochondrial quality control, oxidative stress management, proteostasis and microtubule-based transport mechanisms that are central to Parkinson disease in this curated pathway. The strength of the association is driven primarily by the presence of LRRK2, PINK1 and PARK7, which anchor key directed branches from cellular stress inputs to neuronal degeneration. The intersection is scattered across several pathway segments but shows a concentration in downstream mitochondrial, proteostatic and cytoskeletal effectors, rather than in upstream ligand–receptor modules. Notably, interactions among enriched proteins are reflected in the map, such as coordinated actions of PINK1 and PARK7 on mitochondrial stress responses, the coupling of HSPA5 with ATF4 in ER stress signaling, and the integration of UCHL1 and SNCAIP within ubiquitin-dependent handling of aggregation-prone proteins, collectively outlining a coherent pathogenic cascade in Parkinson disease.

paragraphs: 21 submitted Parkinson disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in a non-intersection pathway component signaling pathway (KEGG:04152).

Among the enriched proteins, the catalytic a non-intersection pathway component subunits PRKAA1 and PRKAA2 and the downstream kinase ULK1 occupy central positions in the canonical KEGG a non-intersection pathway component cascade, linking cellular energy sensing to autophagy initiation. In experimental Parkinson disease models, pharmacological and natural-compound activators of a non-intersection pathway component signaling have been shown to exert neuroprotection, and ULK1 is a key a non-intersection pathway component effector that couples this energy stress signal to autophagic and mitophagic clearance processes that are particularly relevant for dopaminergic neuron survival under mitochondrial toxin exposure. On the KEGG map, PRKAA1 and PRKAA2 sit in the core a non-intersection pathway component complex, upstream of ULK1, placing these proteins on a largely contiguous branch that connects energy sensing directly to autophagy-related outputs in the Parkinson disease–enriched module.

STK11, TSC1, TSC2 and RPTOR form a second set of notable hits that anchor the interface between a non-intersection pathway component and mTOR-dependent growth control. STK11 is the primary upstream kinase for a non-intersection pathway component in this pathway, and in neuronal Parkinson disease models, activation of the STK11–a non-intersection pathway component axis has been reported to mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction and neuronal loss. TSC1 and TSC2 form a complex that integrates a non-intersection pathway component input to restrain the RHEB–RPTOR arm of mTOR signaling, a branch that in turn modulates autophagy and protein synthesis, processes repeatedly implicated in dopaminergic neuron vulnerability; within the KEGG map, these proteins extend the contiguous a non-intersection pathway component branch into the mTOR signaling territory and provide documented cross-talk to the mTOR signaling pathway map.

The remaining enriched proteins fall into several functional clusters. An upstream kinase-activation module comprises STK11 together with its scaffold partners CAB39 and CAB39L, which stabilize and localize the STK11 complex to efficiently activate PRKAA1 and PRKAA2. A regulatory-subunit cluster includes PRKAB1, PRKAB2, PRKAG1, PRKAG2 and PRKAG3, which modulate a non-intersection pathway component activity in response to cellular nucleotide levels and thus tune the strength of downstream responses. A downstream growth-control cluster consists of RHEB and RPTOR, linking the a non-intersection pathway component–TSC1/TSC2 node to mTOR complex function and providing explicit cross-talk with the KEGG mTOR signaling pathway. A transcriptional and metabolic-effector cluster includes FOXO1, FOXO3 and GYS1, which transmit a non-intersection pathway component signals to stress-response transcriptional programs and glycogen metabolism, as well as PPP2R1A, PPP2R2B and PPP2R2D, which represent a non-intersection pathway component components that feedback on kinase cascades within the a non-intersection pathway component map. ULK1, already noted above, also provides cross-talk to the KEGG autophagy map and connects this pathway to mitophagy-related modules highlighted elsewhere in the analysis.

Overall, the enrichment of these 21 proteins in the a non-intersection pathway component signaling pathway indicates that Parkinson disease–related modules are strongly concentrated in the central STK11–a non-intersection pathway component–ULK1 and a non-intersection pathway component–TSC1/TSC2–RHEB–RPTOR branches that couple energy sensing to autophagy and mTOR-regulated growth control. The association appears to be driven primarily by the presence of the core a non-intersection pathway component catalytic subunits PRKAA1 and PRKAA2 together with the upstream kinase STK11, which together define the main signaling axis captured in this pathway. Documented interactions among these proteins, including phosphorylation of PRKAA1/PRKAA2 by STK11, a non-intersection pathway component-mediated regulation of the TSC1/TSC2 complex, inhibitory control of RHEB by TSC1/TSC2, and the recruitment of RPTOR into mTOR complexes, create a contiguous signaling module that links neuronal energy status to pathways of particular relevance for dopaminergic neuron integrity in Parkinson disease.

pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: PI3K-Akt signaling is a major survival and metabolism pathway, and its dysregulation can lower the threshold for dopaminergic neuron death and exacerbate Parkinson disease progression. Modulation of this pathway may influence neuronal resilience to oxidative stress, inflammation, and metabolic insults. 
Intersection-gene interpretation: FOXO3 links PI3K-Akt activity to transcriptional control of stress resistance and apoptosis, while ATF4 connects the pathway to integrated stress responses; CDC37 suggests chaperone-mediated stabilization of kinases within the cascade. GH1 and GYS1 implicate growth hormone signaling and glycogen metabolism as downstream effectors, indicating that altered trophic support and energy handling may shape neuronal vulnerability in Parkinson disease. 
PubMed literature synthesis: The attached studies show that interventions such as hypoxia-preconditioned mesenchymal stem cells, Astragaloside IV, and Wuzi Yanzong pill improve Parkinson disease models in part by engaging or normalizing PI3K-Akt signaling. These findings collectively support a therapeutic concept in which enhancing PI3K-Akt–mediated pro-survival and anti-inflammatory signaling mitigates neurodegeneration.

paragraphs: 26 submitted Parkinson disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt signaling pathway (KEGG:04151).

Within the KEGG a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt map, the enriched proteins cluster predominantly in the central signal transduction modules and downstream effector arms rather than in upstream receptors, with only GH1 representing an upstream hormone input. NFKB1 occupies the inflammatory output branch of a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt signaling and is a core transcription factor in neuroinflammatory responses that are repeatedly reported as modulated via a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt in experimental Parkinson disease models. TSC2 lies on the canonical a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt–to–mTOR axis and functions as a critical inhibitor of RHEB-dependent mTOR activation, thereby linking Akt activity to neuronal growth and stress responses in Parkinson disease–relevant paradigms. PRKAA2, encoding the catalytic subunit of a non-intersection pathway component-activated protein kinase, is positioned in the a non-intersection pathway component–a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt–mTOR interface, where it can restrain mTOR signaling and integrate energetic stress with survival pathways that are frequently targeted by neuroprotective interventions acting through a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt in toxin-induced Parkinson disease models.

Several additional proteins enriched in this pathway refine how a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt signaling is wired in Parkinson disease contexts. RPTOR and RHEB occupy the same downstream mTOR branch as TSC2, indicating that multiple nodes of the a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt–mTOR module are represented and suggesting that altered signaling through this axis is a major contributor to the pathway-level enrichment. STK11, an upstream kinase for PRKAA1 and PRKAA2, further anchors the a non-intersection pathway component branch of the KEGG a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt map, while FOXO3 provides a transcriptional effector of Akt signaling linked to cellular stress resistance in dopaminergic neurons. ATF4 represents a distinct transcriptional endpoint of a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt signaling connected to integrated stress responses, and SGK1 adds an alternative Akt-related kinase effector that converges on ion transport and survival pathways relevant to neuronal resilience in Parkinson disease models that exhibit a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt–dependent neuroprotection.

The remaining enriched proteins fall into several functional clusters along the a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt map. A chaperone/co-chaperone cluster comprising HSP90AA1, HSP90AB1 and CDC37 occupies the central kinase-scaffold region, stabilizing multiple a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt pathway kinases and thereby shaping signal fidelity. A phosphatase-regulatory cluster including PPP2R1A, PPP2R2B and PPP2R2D represents a non-intersection pathway component holoenzyme components that attenuate a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt signaling by dephosphorylating key kinases. A 14-3-3 adaptor cluster, formed by YWHAB, YWHAE, YWHAG, YWHAH, YWHAQ and YWHAZ, overlays broad regulatory control on a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt outputs by binding phosphorylated targets such as transcription factors and mTOR regulators within the KEGG map. IKBKG partners with NFKB1 in the NF-kappa B signaling pathway, a KEGG map that cross-talks extensively with a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt. PRKAA1 joins PRKAA2 and STK11 in the a non-intersection pathway component signaling pathway, while TSC1 complements TSC2, RHEB and RPTOR in the mTOR signaling pathway; together these modules form a largely contiguous branch linking energy sensing to growth control. GYS1 links a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt signaling to glycogen metabolism, and GH1 provides a hormone input into the pathway, underscoring that the enriched proteins are distributed from ligand-level regulation to metabolic and transcriptional outputs rather than confined to a single linear branch.

Overall, the enrichment of these 26 proteins in the a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt signaling pathway indicates that Parkinson disease–related processes strongly engage the interconnected a non-intersection pathway component–mTOR, NF-kappa B and transcriptional effector arms of this pathway rather than isolated upstream receptors. The association appears to be driven primarily by NFKB1, PRKAA2 and TSC2, which together connect inflammatory signaling, energy sensing and mTOR regulation in dopaminergic neurons. The KEGG topology highlights dense cross-talk with the mTOR signaling pathway via TSC1, TSC2, RHEB and RPTOR, with the a non-intersection pathway component signaling pathway via PRKAA1, PRKAA2 and STK11, and with the NF-kappa B signaling pathway via NFKB1 and IKBKG, as well as with the FoxO signaling pathway through FOXO3. Well-documented protein interactions within the enriched set, including the TSC1–TSC2 complex, the binding of HSP90AA1 and HSP90AB1 to CDC37, and the cooperative regulation of TSC2 and FOXO3 by 14-3-3 proteins, provide mechanistic routes by which coordinated perturbation of these nodes could converge on a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt–dependent survival, inflammatory and metabolic responses in Parkinson disease pathology.

pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: Necroptosis is a regulated form of necrotic cell death that promotes inflammation, and accumulating evidence implicates it in neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation in Parkinson disease. Activation of necroptotic machinery in CNS cells can contribute to progressive neuronal loss and chronic inflammatory milieu in PD.
Intersection-gene interpretation: CHMP4B links necroptosis to ESCRT-mediated membrane repair, CYLD deubiquitinates key necroptosis regulators, DNM1L (DRP1) couples mitochondrial dynamics to cell death, and HSP90AA1/HSP90AB1 chaperone necroptotic signalling components. These intersection genes position necroptosis at the crossroads of mitochondrial dysfunction, membrane integrity, and stress-responsive chaperone systems that are all perturbed in PD.
PubMed literature synthesis: The MLKL deficiency study showing alleviated neuroinflammation and motor deficits in an alpha-synuclein PD mouse model, together with reviews on necroptosis and RIPK1-mediated neuroinflammation and on cell death pathways in PD, directly support a pathogenic role for necroptosis in PD. These works indicate that blocking necroptotic signalling can mitigate both inflammatory responses and motor symptoms, highlighting this pathway as a therapeutic target.
Cell/tissue context: The literature specifically implicates CNS cells, including neurons and glial cells, in alpha-synuclein transgenic mouse models of Parkinson disease. [PMID:38041169] [PMID:30467385] [PMID:40712453]

paragraphs: 15 submitted Parkinson disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Necroptosis (KEGG:04217).

Within this map, RIPK1 and RIPK3 occupy the central kinase node of necroptotic signaling downstream of death receptors, where their regulated complex formation governs execution of this form of regulated necrosis. Experimental work in Parkinson disease models and broader CNS disease literature directly implicates RIPK1–RIPK3-mediated necroptosis in dopaminergic neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation, and genetic or pharmacological interference with this axis ameliorates motor deficits and inflammatory responses in alpha-synuclein–driven models, supporting these kinases as key mediators of Parkinson-relevant cell death. In line with this, studies linking miR-425 deficiency to enhanced necroptosis and dopaminergic neuron loss further reinforce the concept that increased activity of the RIPK1–RIPK3 necroptotic machinery is a pathogenic mechanism in Parkinson disease.

TNFRSF1A and TNFRSF10A represent the prototypical upstream death receptors on the KEGG necroptosis map, initiating signaling through their cytoplasmic adaptors to determine whether cells activate survival, apoptosis, or necroptosis. Both receptors are central components of inflammatory cytokine signaling, and necroptosis-focused reviews in Parkinson disease describe how sustained stimulation of such death receptors in the inflamed nigrostriatal environment can bias signaling toward RIPK1-dependent necroptosis, thereby coupling chronic neuroinflammation to dopaminergic neuron death. TRADD and TRAF2, which assemble on TNFRSF1A, occupy the receptor-proximal adaptor layer that scaffolds RIPK1 and modulates its ubiquitination status, and are therefore positioned at a critical decision point between pro-survival and necroptotic complexes in pathways that have been linked to Parkinson-related neurodegeneration.

CYLD, TNFAIP3, USP21 and XIAP form a group of ubiquitin-system regulators that fine-tune the necroptosis node on the KEGG map. CYLD and TNFAIP3 are deubiquitinating enzymes that counteract activating ubiquitin chains on receptor-proximal complexes, restraining pro-survival signaling and thereby promoting conditions permissive for RIPK1–RIPK3 necrosome assembly; necroptosis-focused Parkinson disease reviews highlight this ubiquitin editing of the death-receptor complex as a key molecular switch in dopaminergic neurons under oxidative and inflammatory stress. USP21 adds an additional layer of deubiquitination capacity within this network, reinforcing the prominence of ubiquitin editing in the enriched intersection, while XIAP serves as an E3 ligase and inhibitor of apoptotic caspases that, when dysfunctional or overwhelmed, can shift the balance away from apoptosis and toward necroptosis in degenerating nigral neurons.

The remaining proteins fall into three functionally coherent clusters on the KEGG necroptosis map: a receptor-proximal adaptor and signaling cluster (TRADD, TRAF2, TNFRSF10A), a ubiquitin and cargo-handling cluster (SQSTM1, CYLD, TNFAIP3, USP21, XIAP), and a chaperone–organelle remodeling cluster (HSP90AA1, HSP90AB1, DNM1L, CHMP4B). The adaptor cluster assembles immediately downstream of TNFRSF1A and TNFRSF10A, forming a relatively contiguous block with RIPK1 that integrates inflammatory cues into necroptosis. The ubiquitin and cargo-handling cluster encompasses the ubiquitin-editing enzymes and the selective cargo receptor SQSTM1, which links ubiquitylated necroptotic components to degradative pathways and mediates documented cross-talk from necroptosis into the KEGG autophagy and mitophagy maps. The chaperone–organelle remodeling cluster comprises HSP90AA1 and HSP90AB1, which act as molecular chaperones for necroptotic signaling proteins, together with DNM1L and CHMP4B, which are positioned downstream in executional steps involving mitochondrial fission and membrane remodeling; several of these proteins also provide annotated cross-talk from necroptosis into adjacent KEGG pathways such as tumour-necrosis-factor signalling signaling and apoptosis, reflecting the shared machinery between regulated necrosis and other cell death modalities.

On the KEGG necroptosis map, the intersection proteins are enriched in the tumour-necrosis-factor signalling-family receptor branch, extending from TNFRSF1A and TNFRSF10A through TRADD, TRAF2, and the RIPK1–RIPK3 core, and then into downstream regulatory and executional modules that govern ubiquitin editing, organelle dynamics, and membrane disruption, forming a largely continuous signaling axis rather than scattered, isolated hits. Collectively, these findings support a model in which necroptosis contributes substantially to dopaminergic neuron loss and neuroinflammation in Parkinson disease, with RIPK1, RIPK3 and TNFRSF1A emerging as the principal drivers of the enrichment. Well-documented interactions among the intersection proteins, including the assembly of RIPK1 with RIPK3 at the necrosome, the recruitment of RIPK1 by TRADD and TRAF2 at TNFRSF1A, and the deubiquitination of receptor-proximal complexes by CYLD and TNFAIP3, underscore that these proteins function together as an integrated necroptotic module rather than independent effectors. This coordinated enrichment highlights necroptosis as a central pathway through which inflammatory and oxidative stress signals can converge on regulated cell death in Parkinson disease.

paragraphs: 24 submitted Parkinson disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Programmed Cell Death (REAC:R-HSA-5357801).

In the Reactome event hierarchy, REAC:R-HSA-5357801 is annotated as a pathway-level event within the broader programmed cell death module, with its immediate parent recorded in Reactome as a higher-order programmed cell death event that aggregates more specialized death sub-pathways; the proteins listed for this record are mapped onto the individual reactions and complexes that instantiate this pathway. Within this framework, RIPK1 and RIPK3 act as catalytic serine/threonine kinases in necroptotic signaling branches, forming a kinase complex in the same reaction step that drives execution of regulated necrosis in dopaminergic neurons. TRADD and TRAF2 function as adaptor components of upstream receptor-associated complexes in earlier steps of the same event chain, where they scaffold death receptor signaling that culminates in RIPK1 engagement; this places TRADD/TRAF2-mediated complex assembly and RIPK1/RIPK3 kinase activation in successive, mechanistically linked reactions within the programmed cell death pathway relevant to Parkinson disease.

XIAP is enriched here as a catalytic E3 ubiquitin ligase that suppresses caspase-dependent apoptosis and modulates non-apoptotic forms of programmed cell death; in Reactome it participates as a catalyst and structural component of inhibitor complexes that act downstream of receptor-proximal signaling, in reaction steps that follow those involving RIPK1 and TRADD. TNFRSF10A is annotated as a death receptor that serves as a substrate for ligand binding and a structural hub for a non-intersection pathway component-like complexes, situating it in upstream reactions where it recruits adaptor proteins and initiator enzymes of apoptosis in Parkinson disease models. TP53BP2, in turn, functions as a pro-apoptotic scaffold within this pathway, acting as a component of nuclear and cytoplasmic complexes that integrate stress signals into programmed cell death decisions in neuronal cells, in reactions that are downstream of receptor engagement but upstream of full caspase activation.

Among the proteins that modulate the assembly and stability of death-inducing complexes, HSP90AA1 and CDC37 are enriched as chaperone and co-chaperone components that stabilize catalytic kinases and receptors within programmed cell death signaling; in Reactome they are annotated as components of larger multiprotein complexes rather than as substrates, acting in the same receptor-proximal reaction steps as several of the adaptors. SFN and the closely related STK24 participate as regulatory proteins that tune stress-responsive checkpoints within the pathway, with STK24 acting as a kinase catalyst and SFN as a scaffolding component that binds phospho-targets; these proteins are placed in successive reactions that connect upstream receptor and kinase modules to downstream effector activation in Parkinson disease relevant programmed cell death. DNM1L, which reappears here in a programmed cell death-specific context, is incorporated as a catalytic GTPase in mitochondrial remodeling reactions that lie downstream of death signaling, while CHMP4B is annotated as a structural component of a non-intersection pathway component complexes in membrane scission events that occur in terminal steps of the death program, situating both proteins in late reactions of this pathway rather than in the initial signaling tiers.

CD14 and FLOT2 cluster within membrane-anchored components that organize receptor platforms in innate immune and inflammatory branches of programmed cell death; in Reactome they act as structural components or substrates within receptor-containing complexes that participate in the earliest reaction steps of the event chain, upstream of TRADD and TRAF2 recruitment. C1QBP participates as a component of mitochondrial and possibly nuclear complexes that integrate oxidative stress cues into programmed cell death decisions, in reactions that are topologically downstream of stress-sensing but upstream of full effector engagement in neuronal cells. The cytoskeletal and junctional proteins VIM and DSP are enriched as structural components of intermediate filament and desmosomal assemblies that undergo regulated remodeling as part of cell death execution, acting as substrates in reactions that reflect cytoskeletal reorganization in dopaminergic neuron degeneration. Finally, the 14-3-3 family members YWHAB, YWHAE, YWHAG, YWHAH, YWHAQ, and YWHAZ form a regulatory cluster of phospho-serine/threonine binding scaffold proteins that are annotated as components of multiple signaling complexes across this pathway, frequently occupying the same reaction steps as kinases and apoptotic regulators and thereby modulating the branching between survival and death fates in Parkinson disease models.

Taken together, enrichment of these proteins in REAC:R-HSA-5357801 underscores that multiple, mechanistically distinct programmed cell death routes converge on dopaminergic neuron loss in Parkinson disease, spanning receptor-proximal signaling, mitochondrial and membrane remodeling, and terminal cytoskeletal changes. The association appears to be driven in particular by the necroptotic kinases RIPK1 and RIPK3 and the anti-apoptotic regulator XIAP, which anchor key catalytic and regulatory nodes within this pathway. Well-documented interactions between intersection proteins, such as the formation of RIPK1–RIPK3 kinase complexes and the recruitment of TRADD and TRAF2 to death receptor assemblies containing TNFRSF10A, support a coherent event chain from receptor engagement to multiple programmed cell death outcomes. These findings therefore highlight programmed cell death as an integrated, pathway-level process through which the enriched proteins collectively contribute to Parkinson disease pathology.
